verdict: Too early to call, but the numbers lean its way. Even with a £3,500 battery on top of airbags and bodywork, a hybrid GTS that sells clean around $200,000 leaves room for a rebuilt-title car to pay, provided the purchase price was low [2][4]. The lesson is the bigger story: on the 992.2 a crash that fires the airbags also condemns a sealed battery, and a 911UK staff post warns that can push minor collisions toward uneconomic [2]. Hybrids make the salvage arithmetic harsher.
body:
## The buy

Saving Salvage, the British channel that rebuilds crashed new cars, has taken on a 992.2-generation Porsche 911 Carrera GTS, the first 911 with Porsche's T-Hybrid system [3][6]. The first episode calls it brand new and crashed [3]. Where it was bought and for how much hasn't appeared in any text we could read, so the purchase price here is unknown. The channel's previous project on file, a mangled Audi RS3, turned out better underneath than it looked; this one has gone the other way.

The 992.2 GTS pairs a new 3.6-liter flat-six and an electrically driven turbocharger with a small battery and a motor in the gearbox [6]. That hybrid hardware is the problem.

## The damage

Part two, posted October 13, asks in its title whether buying the car was a mistake, and its description says hybrid cars have made things very difficult to repair [1]. The detail came out on the 911UK forum, where a member summarized the video: when the airbags deploy in a crash, a pyrotechnic fuse inside the high-voltage battery blows [2]. The battery is welded shut, so the fuse can't be replaced on its own; the whole pack has to go [2]. A forum staff member described the battery as about 400 volts and 1.9 kWh, liquid-cooled and made by Rimac [2].

That staff post drew the wider conclusion: a front-end or even minor collision that trips the high-voltage cut-off can make a 992.2 GTS much more expensive to repair, or uneconomic [2]. Another staff note pointed out that combustion Porsches also use pyrotechnic battery terminals linked to the airbags, though those are usually cheap to replace [2]. The extent of the body damage on this car hasn't been described in text.

## The work and the parts

The one firm number is the battery. The video put the cost at £3,500 for a dealer to supply, fit and code a new pack, per the forum [2]; that's about $4,550 at roughly $1.30 to the pound, our conversion. Against a car that sells for around $200,000 clean, that's a manageable number.

The rest of the list follows from the crash. Airbags that fired have to be replaced with their pretensioners, and the bodywork has to be repaired; neither has been priced. We've listed them with no cost rather than guess.

## The money

In: unknown purchase price, plus £3,500 for the battery, plus airbags and body repairs.

Out: a clean hybrid GTS is a $200,000 car in America. A Philadelphia dealer sold a 1,189-mile 2025 GTS T-Hybrid cabriolet at $199,000 [4], classic.com's 15 priced listings of 992.2 Carrera GTS cars averaged about $229,000 in asking price, with Porsche Annapolis asking $214,055 in October 2025 [5], and a 2023 GTS of the previous generation made $212,000 on Bring a Trailer after the auction [7]. In Britain a repaired write-off carries a Category S or N marker, the equivalent of a rebuilt title, and buyers usually take 20% to 40% off for it. On that basis we put the finished car at $120,000 to $160,000 in U.S. terms. We haven't checked UK prices, where the channel would sell it.

## What's next

With the battery issue understood, the remaining work is the airbags, the body repair and getting the hybrid system to run cleanly with its new pack. The forum thread had an update post on October 20 with no details [2]. We'll add the purchase price, the parts and the outcome as Saving Salvage states them.
